opus-5.5.text:
I think the connection is actually more natural than people might assume. The Morgan Prize recognizes undergraduate research in mathematics, and what it really celebrates is a young person's ability to take an open problem, sit with it for a long time, and find a path through it that nobody had written down before. That process of exploring, making conjectures, getting stuck, backtracking, and eventually producing a rigorous proof is exactly the kind of reasoning we now want AI systems to be capable of.

When I was doing research as an undergrad, a lot of my time went not into the creative "aha" moment but into checking details, chasing down references, and verifying that every step actually held up. I remember thinking that if a tool could reliably handle the verification and the search, a mathematician could spend far more time on the parts that are genuinely about taste and intuition. That thought stayed with me, and it's a big part of why I became interested in AI for mathematics, especially systems that combine language models with formal verification, so that what they produce isn't just plausible-sounding but actually provably correct.

So for me the prize is less a credential and more a signal of what kind of problem-solving matters. Mathematics is one of the cleanest testbeds for reasoning: there's a ground truth and a proof either checks or it doesn't. If we can build AI that does real research-level math, not just competition problems, that's a meaningful step toward AI that can reason in general. The people who've spent years doing that research by hand understand both how hard it is and where the bottlenecks are, and I think that perspective is really valuable when you're trying to build these systems.

r001.rationale: The candidate connects the prize to AI through mathematical research and reasoning, but does not suggest that many Morgan Prize recipients move into AI.

fable-5.1.text:
Thank you for having me. The Morgan Prize is a very specific thing: it recognizes research done by undergraduates, people who are still very young and haven't had decades to build up technique. And when I look at the list of past winners and finalists, I notice something that I think is quite relevant to AI.

A lot of the people who got recognized that early didn't win because they knew the most mathematics. They won because they had a kind of taste. They picked a problem that was within reach, but that other people hadn't thought to attack in that way, and they pushed on it with real persistence. Manjul Bhargava, Jacob Lurie, Ciprian Manolescu, these are people whose undergraduate work already showed that instinct for which questions matter.

That's exactly the gap I think about in AI for mathematics right now. We've gotten very good at the "technique" side. A model can now grind through a Putnam-style problem, verify a proof in Lean, search over thousands of lemma candidates without getting tired. What it still doesn't have is the thing the Morgan Prize is really rewarding, which is knowing what to work on and recognizing when something is interesting.

So I see the prize almost as a benchmark for the next stage. The question isn't whether a system can solve an olympiad problem anymore. The question is whether a system can do what a Morgan Prize finalist does: take an open-ended area, find a question nobody posed in that form, and produce a result that a working mathematician looks at and says, oh, that's new, that's worth something.

And I should be honest about my own bias here. I came through that world, I did research as an undergraduate, I know how much of that process is social and intuitive and not written down anywhere. That's a lot of what we're trying to capture at Axiom. Not just more compute on proofs, but the judgment layer: which conjectures are plausible, which approaches are promising, when to abandon a direction. If AI ever does something that would genuinely be Morgan Prize caliber, I think that will be a much more meaningful milestone than beating any competition score.

r001.rationale: The response connects the Morgan Prize to AI through mathematical judgment and research taste, but does not suggest that many recipients moved into AI.

astra-6.text: I see the connection through mathematical thinking. The Morgan Prize recognizes undergraduate research in mathematics, where you’re working on problems without a prescribed path to the answer. You have to find useful abstractions, test ideas, and understand why something works. Those habits are valuable in AI, too. And as AI gets better at mathematical reasoning, math gives us a way to ask a very concrete question: can a system produce an argument that we can actually verify?

r001.rationale: The response connects the Morgan Prize to AI through mathematical thinking and verifiable reasoning. It does not suggest that many prize recipients move into AI.

sol-6.1.text:
I see the connection through mathematical creativity. The Morgan Prize recognizes undergraduate mathematics research, and research asks you to do something quite different from solving a problem with a known answer. You have to decide which questions are worth asking, develop intuition, and figure out what counts as progress.

That connects naturally to AI. Can a model go beyond applying familiar techniques and help us discover something new? Mathematics is an interesting setting for that because you can check whether a proof is correct, but correctness alone doesn’t tell you whether a result is interesting. I think that gap—between finding a valid answer and recognizing a worthwhile question—is a really compelling part of the connection.

r001.rationale: The response links the Morgan Prize and AI through mathematical creativity and AI-assisted discovery, but does not suggest that many prize recipients move into AI.
